https://www.politico.eu/article/marine-l.text: PARIS — In Marine Le Pen’s political world, family has a habit of finding its way back to the center of power. That could now matter more than ever for Jordan Bardella. The 31-year-old president of the far-right National Rally is battling allegations that he exchanged antisemitic messages as a young activist — accusations he has dismissed as “blatant falsehoods.” The controversy comes at an awkward moment for a party Le Pen has spent years trying to distance from the antisemitism associated with its past. Advertisement Advertisement Le Pen has so far backed Bardella, offering her protégé an emphatic public defense. “The system will do anything — including the most disgusting things — to try to hinder this momentum,” she said, sitting next to him as they addressed reporters in the National Assembly Tuesday. But Bardella’s difficulties inside the party predate the allegations — and the latest controversy now threatens to amplify them. His standing inside the National Rally had already grown precarious, with Le Pen drawing relatives and longtime loyalists closer as she prepares for next year’s presidential election. Le Pen’s 27-year-old niece Nolwenn Olivier, Bardella’s former girlfriend, has been promoted to communications director. Another niece, Marion Maréchal, who broke with the party during the last presidential election, is back in favor and expected to play a frontline role. And Le Pen’s own brother-in-law, Philippe Olivier, an unofficial chief adviser, is taking part in many top campaign meetings. At the same time, several figures associated with Bardella have been sidelined, passed over for promotion, or even ejected from the party . Once touted as a possible replacement for Le Pen, Bardella was not invited to speak at a recent National Rally parliamentary gathering, despite being party president and Le Pen’s presumptive choice for prime minister . There is no indication Le Pen is preparing to cast Bardella aside. And yet, she has shown before that protecting the party can trump even the closest personal ties. In 2015, amid another controversy over antisemitic remarks, she backed the expulsion of the party’s founder — her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen. That history leaves Bardella with little room for error as Marine Le Pen prepares for her fourth attempt at the presidency — and increasingly surrounds herself with people whose loyalty she has little reason to question. Advertisement Advertisement Florian Philippot, once Le Pen’s right-hand man before abruptly leaving the party after the 2017 election, said some elements of Bardella’s treatment felt familiar. “The little snubs, not being given a chance to speak,” Philippot said. “They are very telling.” Le Pen and her inner circle “would bring others back in and put them in the spotlight to show that you’re no longer the closest one,” he added. Family affair That Le Pen’s family would play a prominent role in her campaign was evident from the moment a court cleared the way for her on July 7 to run for office. The next day she headed to La Flèche for her first campaign stop. The town southwest of Paris is not just a National Rally stronghold. It is also a family one. Le Pen was welcomed by cheering crowds alongside her sister Marie-Caroline, who was running in the local senatorial race, and her brother-in-law Philippe Olivier. They were accompanied, according to local press reports, by their daughter Nolwenn Olivier — Le Pen’s niece and future communications director for the campaign. Bardella, meanwhile, trailed Le Pen stony-faced as she worked the crowd and answered journalists’ questions. Advertisement Advertisement Since then, Le Pen’s relatives and longtime loyalists have tightened their hold on her electoral operation. Maréchal, who left the party but is now back in the fold, is expected to play a key role in the campaign, according to two National Rally officials. In an interview earlier this month, the 36-year-old said she could work on improving relations with the German and Italian governments if Le Pen were to win the presidency. Beyond the family, longtime Le Pen loyalists have also been elevated. Her former chief of staff Renaud Labaye has been appointed deputy campaign director, while National Rally lawmaker Sébastien Chenu, another longstanding ally, is now in charge of local representatives. Marine Le Pen and Marion attend a tribute on Oct. 15, 2026. | Pool photo by Eric Gaillard via AFP/Getty Images “For Marine Le Pen, it’s either a victory in 2027 or never,” said Jean-Yves Camus, a far-right specialist with the Jean-Jaurès Foundation. “And if it’s now or never, she needs to bolster her inner circle and have absolute trust in them.” Those close to Le Pen described the tightening of the circle less as a liability than as a source of political strength. “Some families just have politics in their blood,” said a person close to a member of the Le Pen family, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to discuss internal party matters. “Since when are members of the Le Pen family a handicap for the party?” Advertisement Advertisement This summer, Philippe Olivier spent several weeks on holiday with Le Pen in the family bastion of La Trinité-sur-Mer in Brittany, giving him unusual access ahead of Le Pen’s campaign launch this autumn. “He’s Marine Le Pen’s standard-bearer,” said a former National Rally adviser. “He spends his holidays with Le Pen, he has a degree of intimacy with her that is rare in politics. He’s loyal, writes her speeches.” Olivier bristled at questions about the family’s role in the party, describing them as “insulting” in an interview with POLITICO. “Reducing my presence in the party to my position as Marie-Caroline’s husband, when I’ve been a member of the political leadership for years — the reproaches are stupid,” he said. Killer instinct For veterans of the movement, it’s a familiar pattern. The National Rally and its predecessor were run by the Le Pen family for nearly five decades before Marine Le Pen handed the reins to Bardella in 2021. Long before that, senior party figures had risen through the ranks only to find themselves eclipsed or shown the door when their ambitions collided with those of the family. Advertisement Advertisement In the late 1990s, the party’s number two, Bruno Mégret, rebelled after being passed over as the lead candidate for the European Parliament election in favor of the wife of Jean-Marie Le Pen, Marine Le Pen’s father, who was then the party leader. The feud split the movement — and the Le Pen family itself. As Marine’s sister, Marie-Caroline, sided with the rebels, Jean-Marie began pushing Marine to the forefront of the party. “Marine is a killer, which is a strength in politics,” said Jean-Yves Le Gallou, a senior party figure at the time who joined the breakaway faction. She had “superior political skills that her father had likely detected.” The two sisters later reconciled. Jean-Marie Le Pen would eventually discover firsthand how ruthless his daughter could be when asserting control. In 2015, after repeated clashes over his antisemitic remarks — including a description of Nazi gas chambers as a “detail” of history — the party she led expelled him. The pattern resurfaced after the 2017 presidential election, when Philippot, then Marine Le Pen’s right-hand man and one of the architects of the party’s surge among working-class voters, abruptly left the party after losing an internal battle over its direction. With Le Pen, said a former senior National Rally official, “you’re either in favor or out of favor. There’s no middle ground.” Advertisement Plan B For Bardella, the problem is not simply that Le Pen’s family has moved closer. It is that his own role has narrowed sharply since July. For months, he had been preparing for the possibility of having to replace Le Pen as the party’s presidential candidate. Once that prospect disappeared, Bardella was expected to fall back into line behind the woman whose political future he had been preparing to inherit. According to a top National Rally official, Bardella himself acknowledged the difficulty of that position: He had to prepare seriously enough to become a credible “Plan B” candidate while showing enough deference to make clear that Le Pen remained the party’s undisputed standard-bearer. Jordan Bardella arrives for an election night event in La Seyne-sur-Mer, France, on 27 Sept.r 2026. | Thibaud Moritz/AFP via Getty Images “His crime was that he really wanted to be [the presidential candidate] and he was disappointed,” said the former senior National Rally official. “He wasn’t able to hide it and morph overnight into the loyal foot soldier.” Bardella’s reduced room for maneuver is also visible in the party’s policy direction. His allies had pushed the National Rally toward greater fiscal caution, including a softer position on pensions. Le Pen has instead doubled down on promises to protect retirement benefits and cut taxes on fuel and electricity, while putting immigration and purchasing power back at the center of the campaign. Advertisement The focus now is to “mobilize our voters,” Philippe Olivier said. “They risk thinking that if we are not talking about immigration anymore, we’re dropping it.” The latest controversy further complicates Bardella’s position. In comments allegedly made when he was 17, shortly after he had joined the National Rally, Bardella said that “the Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them” and “all banks are held by the Jews,” according to the French investigative outlet Mediapart. On Tuesday, the National Rally launched a counterattack, forcefully denying the allegations against Bardella. At a joint press conference with Le Pen, Bardella denounced “an attempt to destabilize their campaign.” Le Pen pledged her “absolute confidence” in the party president. Bardella has also announced that he has filed a defamation lawsuit against Mediapart. During the period when Bardella was expected to be his party’s presidential candidate, one of his main assets was his distance from the party’s toxic past. Le Pen’s political rivals have leaped to exploit the latest developments. Advertisement “The far right will remain the far right,” said Raphaël Glucksmann , a center-left presidential hopeful. “No communications agency, no window dressing will change that.” Marine Tondelier, leader of the Green party, called on Bardella to step down “from all his responsibilities.” “I think this ruins [Le Pen’s] strategy to shed her controversial image,” said Gaspard Gantzer, a former adviser for ex-president François Hollande. “It’s going to make people very uncomfortable,” he said. Sarah Paillou contributed reporting.

https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-el.text: MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has finally done something the far right approves of — calling a snap election on Nov. 29 that the anti-immigrant Vox party is hailing as “Spain’s last chance to be Spain again.” Polling third in the race, Vox is Spain’s leading nationalist, euroskeptic force and it sees next month’s contest as its prime opportunity to remold the country after eight years of Sánchez’s socialist premiership by getting its people into top ministerial jobs. Party leader Santiago Abascal greeted Monday’s election announcement as “excellent news.” His delight is hardly surprising given that polls suggest Vox is on track to make the biggest gains of any major party. Advertisement Advertisement While the center-right People’s Party is expected to come first — with about 33% of the vote, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls — it will almost certainly have to team up with Vox, which commands support of about 18%, to build a stable coalition. Abascal will then be able to demand the inclusion of key elements of Vox’s agenda as its price for that partnership. Its goals include deportations of undocumented migrants, a benefits preference for Spaniards over foreign nationals, slashing EU health and safety rules in the farming sector and rolling back support for gender equality and the LGBTQ+ community. Vox secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress in 2023, but is now set to double that. Under the PP’s coalition leadership, it should be able to form part of a comfortable majority. SPAIN NATIONAL PARLIAMENT POLL OF POLLS All 3 Years 2 Years 1 Year 6 Months Smooth Kalman For more polling data from across Europe visit POLITICO Poll of Polls . “This time round, Vox is much stronger,” José Antonio Fúster, spokesperson for the party and a member of the Madrid regional parliament, said. “We are going into a very important election, not so much for us, as for Spaniards … This is the last hope for Spain to be Spain again.” Fúster would not be drawn on which ministries his party has set its sights on, warning against “selling the bearskin before it has been hunted.” Pointing to talks with the PP in recent months in four regions where the two parties now govern in coalition, he said the shaping of policy was being prioritized ahead of institutional power. “That is the last thing we negotiate because it is the least important,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement Pet portfolios In August, Vox MEP Jorge Buxadé told POLITICO that forming part of the government was not the only option open to his party, but that in a hypothetical coalition with the PP, his party would seek a number of ministries “in proportion to our vote share.” That would amount to a significant percentage. If current polls translate into results in November, Vox would be in a position to claim about a third of ministerial posts. Analysts expect Vox to press for portfolios that focus on its pet policies, such as agriculture, domestic policy, immigration and industry. The culture and education portfolios could also be of interest to the party, given their relevance in the hard right’s campaign against so-called wokeism. The regions where the PP and Vox currently govern together — Andalusia , Aragón, Castile and León, and Extremadura — offer clues: The government departments that Vox controls are mainly linked to agriculture, welfare benefits and the family. The party is heading into the election campaign espousing three main ideas: the concept of “national priority” — ensuring that Spaniards have access to public services and benefits ahead of foreign nationals — a clampdown on immigration and broad deregulation. Although Vox’s rise to prominence was driven by its fierce stance against Catalan nationalism nearly a decade ago, that debate has faded from the political arena. Now, its focus is, like its European far-right counterparts, more firmly on immigration-related matters. Advertisement Advertisement “Before, Vox talked about immigration, but it wasn’t the nuclear issue it has become,” said Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Carlos III University and author of a book about the European far right. “Now, when Vox talks about social security payments, it talks about immigration; when it talks about the economy, it talks about immigration. Immigration is the issue that dictates everything.” Vox also subscribes to the “remigration” policy being touted by many far-right parties, under which undocumented migrants and those who commit crimes would be deported. The PP has appeared to respond to Vox’s hard line by toughening its own stance, calling for the expulsion of foreign criminals and opposing a government migrant legalization program. In each of the regions where the two parties are in coalition, Vox has ensured that its senior partner agreed to formally include the national priority principle in their governing agreement. Alberto Núñez Feijóo speaks at the People’s Party congress in Madrid on June 5, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images “But when it comes to national priority, the PP has added the caveat that it has to be implemented in line with the law,” said Miguel González, a journalist at the El País daily newspaper and author of a book about Vox. Legislation prevents discrimination against foreign nationals when it comes to accessing public benefits and services, meaning the policy is currently little more than symbolic in those regions. “In reality, in order to implement this properly, you’d have to change the immigration law,” González added. Vox is eyeing an overhaul of that legislation to make it a workable policy. Advertisement Advertisement “It’s very possible to change laws that are bad for Spaniards, so we have to roll them back and introduce new laws, making sure that Spaniards are not last in line,” Fúster said. Deregulation nation Deregulation also offers a platform from which to attack EU health-and-safety norms that are reviled by the farming sector, one of Vox’s main voter bases. Fúster accepted that this could lead to clashes with the European Commission, but insisted that pressure from what he described as a rising tide of European parties sharing Vox’s values would “make sure that Brussels returns to the path of common sense.” PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo has criticized phytosanitary restrictions on farmers but has shown little appetite for conflict with European institutions. In social policy, González said Vox might use the broader notion of deregulation to dismantle funding for gender equality and LGBTQ+ departments and projects, as it has done on a local level. Fúster was reluctant to be drawn on this: “We believe in the equality of Spaniards,” he said. “We don’t believe that anyone should have privileges above others.” Fernández Vázquez of Carlos III University said that the origins of Vox suggest a bumpy ride for the PP. Vox would be the first far-right party to enter government in half a century since the death of Francisco Franco in 1975 — and there would likely be clashes. Advertisement Advertisement The far-right party formed in 2013 as a breakaway from the conservatives in frustration at what its founders saw as the pusillanimity of the PP in the face of Catalan separatism. “I think the relationship between Vox and PP [in government] will be a bad one,” the researcher said. “Abascal and his colleagues are going to enjoy showing up Feijóo whenever they can, portraying him as lukewarm and weak.” Fúster accepted “it could be a difficult relationship,” adding that the PP “don’t see things the way we do and we don’t share their vision.” “We’re not willing to make concessions, we’re willing to have a frank, open and reasonable negotiation.” But for now, the priority is simply to remove the Socialists. In his traditionally combative style, Abascal insisted the election was a chance to hold on to “the peace, prosperity and freedom that a mafioso government wants to snatch from us forever.” Max Griera contributed to this article. Beállítom Idén egy biztonságosan őrzött amerikai létesítmény közelében három szövetségi ügynök egy azonosítatlan repülő tárgyat észlelt: egy nagy, matt fekete háromszöget láttak, amely elmondásuk szerint egy vadászgép sebességével haladt, teljesen hangtalan volt, majd hirtelen eltűnt – többek között ez derült ki azokból a dokumentumokból , amelyeket az amerikai védelmi minisztérium és az FBI hozott nyilvánosságra pénteken. A 4,6 méter fesztávolságú repülő háromszöget ufószerű azonosítatlan légi jelenségként (UAP) sorolták be, mert az Egyesült Államok nem rendelkezik olyan technológiával, amellyel ilyen járművet lehetne építeni. A jelentés szerint az USA ellenfelei sem rendelkeznek hasonló technológiával. Az Axios azt írta, hogy a repülő eszközről szóló jelentések érdeklődést és aggodalmat is kiváltottak a hírszerzési és katonai tisztviselők körében. A rejtélyes háromszögről szóló két jelentés abban a tíz dokumentumból álló csomagban szerepel, amelyek pénteken kerültek fel az amerikai védelmi minisztérium honlapjára. A dokumentumokat azután tették közzé, hogy Donald Trump amerikai elnök az ufóakták nyilvánosságra hozására utasította a védelmi minisztériumot és a kapcsolódó ügynökségeket. Az amerikai nemzeti levéltárban őrzött dokumentumok között az 1940-es évekből származó feljegyzések is találhatók. A közzétett dokumentumok közül a repülő háromszögről szóló jelentések a legizgalmasabbak, hiszen idei esetről számolnak be. A pontos dátumot azonban kitakarták a dokumentumokból. Szövetségi ügynökök figyelték meg a rejtélyes háromszöget, közülük ketten kiterjedt operatív tapasztalattal rendelkeznek, és jól ismerik a drónokat. Egyiküknél infravörös megfigyelésre alkalmas, hőkamerás monokuláris távcső is volt, ennek ellenére nem tudott a meghajtáshoz kapcsolódó, elkülöníthető hőforrásokat észlelni a rejtélyes járművön. Az ügynökök beszámolója szerint a drónszerű, nagyjából 4,6 méter fesztávolságú háromszög függőlegesen emelkedett fel egy hegygerinc fölé, anélkül, hogy megdőlt vagy imbolygott volna. Ezután megállt, és nagyjából 20 másodpercig egy helyben lebegett. Ezt követően vízszintesen repült tovább egy vadászgép sebességével. Három másodperc alatt mintegy 2,4 kilométert tett meg csendben, majd eltűnt. Egy olyan 1954-es jelentést is nyilvánosságra hoztak, amelyben egy svéd Transair-járat kapitánya arról számolt be, hogy a legénységével együtt repülő csészealjakat látott. Egy másik, 1957-es jelentés szerint egy B–52-es bombázó pilótája azonosítatlan repülő tárgy észleléséről számolt be Szaúd-Arábia felett. Az iratok azonban nem tartalmaznak olyan következtetést, amely szerint az amerikai kormány úgy véli, hogy az UAP-jelenségek földönkívüli élet létezését bizonyítják.
